analysis.one_liner: Requires states to make hospitals disclose their charges and insurers to estimate patients' out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee in March 2013 and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state, as a condition of its Medicaid program, to pass laws forcing hospitals to disclose what they charge for inpatient and outpatient services and make that information available to people seeking care. It would also have required health insurers — including Medicaid managed care and Medicare Advantage plans — to give customers an estimate of what they would pay out of pocket for upcoming care on request. Finally, it directed the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to study what price information consumers actually find useful and report to Congress within 18 months. The bill gave states flexibility rather than imposing federal standards, and it made clear that the estimates would not be binding guarantees of what a patient ultimately pays.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients — especially uninsured and Medicaid patients who face hospital bills directly — would gain access to hospital charge information, and anyone with insurance could ask their plan for an estimate of what a given service would cost them before receiving it. That kind of advance price information is what lets people compare hospitals, question surprise bills, and avoid charges that bear no relation to what care actually costs. States would also gain federal research on how to present price information in a usable form.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients comparing hospital and insurance costs

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals would be required to disclose charges for selected inpatient and outpatient services and provide timely public access to that information, so patients could see prices before getting care.

Anyone with health coverage could request an estimate of the out-of-pocket costs they would likely face for a particular service, from their insurer, Medicaid managed care organization, or Medicare Advantage plan.

The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality would research which price and cost information consumers find useful and report to Congress within 18 months with recommendations for how the federal government could help states.
The bill set no federal standards for the state laws, letting states keep or adapt existing disclosure programs rather than forcing uniform rules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals would bear the cost of compiling and publishing charge data, and their long-standing ability to keep prices obscure — which lets different patients pay very different amounts for the same care — would be curtailed. Health insurers would bear the cost of producing individualized out-of-pocket estimates on request, and to the extent transparency fuels price competition, both hospitals and insurers would face pressure on the margins they earn from opaque pricing. Federal spending on the AHRQ research would be subject to appropriation.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure of hospital 'charges' is a weak measure of real prices: hospitals routinely set inflated list charges that few patients actually pay, and uninsured patients may not be able to negotiate down to the rates insurers get, so published charges could confuse more than inform.

The bill explicitly did not guarantee that a patient's actual costs would stay within the estimate an insurer provides, so the out-of-pocket statements would be non-binding and could still leave patients with surprise bills.

It imposed the requirements as conditions tied to state Medicaid plans with no federal uniform standards, so the strength of disclosure would vary widely from state to state depending on each state's politics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a modest, real step for patients rather than a sweeping fix. Published hospital charges and non-binding cost estimates would not by themselves control prices or eliminate surprise bills — the bill itself acknowledged estimates could be exceeded. But it cost taxpayers almost nothing beyond a research authorization, and it would have shifted one piece of leverage to patients: the ability to see what care costs before choosing where to get it. The main weakness is that it relied entirely on state legislatures to write and enforce the disclosure laws.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Burgess introduced the bill on March 21, 2013, joined by Representatives Gene Green and John Carter, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken — no markup, no committee or floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill drew four cosponsors, three Republicans and one Democrat, giving it bipartisan but thin support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers came out ahead: the pricing practices the bill would have exposed — hospital charges that stay hidden from patients and insurance costs that surface only after treatment — remained in place, and patients never got the advance price information.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers kept prices private

sides.party_line_note: The small sponsorship was bipartisan — three Republicans and one Democrat backing a Republican sponsor — and no vote ever occurred, so party lines were never tested on the floor.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish charges for selected services, ending the secrecy that lets the same procedure carry wildly different bills and leaves patients unable to comparison-shop. Public price visibility pressures hospitals toward lower, more consistent pricing.

industries.industry: Health insurers, including Medicaid managed care and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: Insurers would face new administrative work producing individualized out-of-pocket estimates on request, and advance cost information would help patients compare plans and question bills. The bill explicitly brought Medicaid managed care and Medicare Advantage plans under the state disclosure laws.
A small cost: the AHRQ research would have been funded by appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary'.
